title: Wild parrots exhibit age-dependent conformity when learning about novel food
experiments_summary:
The study was conducted on urban sulphur-crested cockatoos (Cacatua galerita) at five roosting communities in central Sydney, Australia. Birds were individually marked with nontoxic dye in unique color combinations, and feather samples were collected for genetic sexing. Social association data were gathered via group scans (every 10 minutes, 864 total scans) across two observation periods before and after the main experiment, and a social network was constructed using the simple ratio index via the gambit-of-the-group approach. Roost membership was determined through three roost-counts per site.

For the main cultural diffusion experiment, two adult pairs at two roosts (Balmoral Beach, BA; Clifton Gardens, CG) were trained as demonstrators: the BA pair was trained to eat blue-dyed unshelled almonds and the CG pair was trained to eat red-dyed unshelled almonds, using a stepwise desensitization protocol. A third roost (Northbridge, NB) served as an untrained control. Over 10 days, a dispenser containing both red and blue almonds was presented daily at each roost; sessions were filmed using a fixed camcorder and presence scans were taken every 10 minutes. Individual choices (color selected, identity, time) were coded from videos using BORIS software.

Because BA demonstrators lost their trained blue preference on day one, the experiment was extended to two secondary roosts (Manly, MA; Royal Botanic Gardens, BG) over a second 10-day period. No new demonstrators were trained; instead, the protocol relied on naturally moving knowledgeable individuals to introduce the behavior. These secondary sites were initially presented only with blue almonds until sufficient consumption occurred, then red almonds were added.

To assess whether spread of novel food consumption followed the social network, a network-based diffusion analysis (NBDA) was performed using order-of-acquisition diffusion analysis (OADA) with multiple diffusions. Models with and without social transmission were compared across all combinations of individual-level variables (age, sex) using AICc.

To investigate social learning strategies for color choice, experience-weighted attraction (EWA) models were fit. Five models were compared: pure individual reinforcement learning, and four models combining individual learning with one of four social biases (frequency-dependent/conformity, male-bias, same-roost-bias, age-bias). Models incorporated individual and group-level heterogeneity by age and sex class, used a 60-second observation window prior to each solve, and were fit using Stan via cmdstanr with 4 chains and 1,000 sampling plus 1,000 warm-up iterations. Model comparison used WAIC.

Almond opening techniques were opportunistically filmed using a handheld camera across all five roosts. From 539 opening sequences of 147 individuals, three behavioral variables were coded: presence of optional outer-shell removal (unshelling), location of first crack, and extraction method. A dissimilarity matrix was computed from these variables using Euclidean distance, and four partial Mantel tests were conducted to assess the effects of individual identity, geographic distance between roosts, movement rates between roosts, and social association strength on similarity of opening sequences, each controlling for the other predictors.
